title: Lesson 26: Auditing AI Use on a Regular Cadence
description: Grounded in Lesson 26 of the AI Adoption series: what an AI audit is, why it has to run on a regular cadence rather than from memory, the difference between an audit and continuous monitoring, and the four-item scope (inventory, policy, licenses and spend, policy currency) a non-technical owner uses to check whether AI governance still reflects reality.

questions.question: How does a scheduled audit differ from continuous monitoring?
options: The audit checks on a schedule whether controls and records still match reality
The audit watches signals in real time and alerts someone when a threshold has been crossed
The audit samples the logs that monitoring already collected and reports on them
The audit reviews the budget instead of the tools, seats, and access in use
questions.explanation: Monitoring watches continuously for a line being crossed, while an audit steps back on a schedule to ask whether the lines themselves are still the right ones.

questions.question: An audit that starts from opinions rather than records is weak because:
options: It takes far longer to run than an audit built on a fixed list of specific evidence pulls
It duplicates work that continuous monitoring already does in real time
It measures whether people objected in a meeting rather than whether the rules held
It cannot be placed on a calendar, so it tends to happen only once a year
questions.explanation: An audit is only as strong as the records it compares against expectations; without named evidence it becomes a discussion about intentions.

questions.question: How should the interval between audits be set?
options: Every system is checked on the same annual cycle so the process stays simple
High-risk systems are checked more often, and every interval has a scheduled date
The interval stays open so checks happen whenever someone notices a problem worth raising
Only the cheapest tools are checked, since waste is the main risk with AI tools
questions.explanation: Review intensity follows risk, and the real requirement is a date on the calendar, because a check that depends on memory is not a cadence.
